passage:
Monday. Noor got to her father's flat at eight, tired from work, and found his tablets mixed in the wrong compartments. "Abbu, I asked you to call me!" she snapped. His eyes dropped, and her stomach dropped with them. At home, her husband Thomas was eating dinner alone again.

Saturday. On a video call, Noor's brother Farhan took the Sunday doctor visits and the pharmacy; Noor kept weekday evenings; Thomas offered to drive on Thursdays. Then Noor asked Abbu what he wanted. "I'll fill my own tablet box," he said. "You can check it once a week."

Two Tuesdays later, Abbu showed her the box, every compartment right. Noor glanced over it, then stayed for chai, and was home by eight to eat with Thomas.

qa.q: Who took over the Sunday doctor visits and the pharmacy?
qa.a: Noor's brother Farhan took the Sunday doctor visits and the pharmacy.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling on the first Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was tired and stretched thin, which spilled into a sharp remark. Her stomach dropping when Abbu's eyes dropped suggests she regretted it at once.

qa.q: How did the new arrangement protect Abbu's dignity?
qa.a: Abbu chose to fill his own tablet box with only a weekly check, so he was treated as a capable adult rather than someone being managed.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt when Noor snapped at him about the tablets?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed, as if he were being scolded like a child, which his lowered eyes suggest.

grounding: Shows an adult child balancing work, spouse and care duties, splitting tasks with a sibling and keeping her father's dignity over three days.

passage:
Kunal, you ask how I managed when my mother fell ill. I was twenty-five, newly married, and just promoted.

Amma had a stroke that winter. I wanted to do everything myself: leave early, sleep at the hospital, cancel work. In two weeks I was snapping at your aunt Mala and falling asleep in meetings.

My sister Rekha stopped me. "You're not the only child," she said. So we sat down with paper: I took doctor visits and bills, Rekha took mornings, our younger brother took Sundays. Mala said she would do Amma's hair every evening, because Amma always liked it neat.

The part I'm proudest of? Amma couldn't use her right hand well, but she still chose her own saris each day, even if it took twenty minutes. We waited. It was her life.

That's what your old Chetan Mama learned: share the load, and let the person stay themselves.

qa.q: What did Mala offer to do every evening?
qa.a: Mala offered to do Amma's hair every evening.

qa.q: How did young Chetan feel in the first two weeks of Amma's illness?
qa.a: Chetan felt overwhelmed and exhausted, snapping at Mala and falling asleep in meetings from trying to do everything alone.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how young Chetan handled the care?
qa.a: When Rekha said he wasn't the only child, they split tasks on paper among the siblings and Mala.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt being allowed to choose her own saris?
qa.a: Amma likely felt respected and still herself, keeping dignity and choice despite her illness.

grounding: Shows through an elder's memory how a young adult balances work, spouse and care, splits tasks with siblings and keeps the parent's dignity.

The client presentation was at ten, and at seven Pradeep's father called: he had fallen in the bathroom again, not badly, but he was shaken. His wife Yamini had worked a night shift at the hospital and was just getting home.

Pradeep felt pulled three ways. He drove over first, sat with his father on the edge of the bed, and helped him check his knee.

"Don't fuss," his father said. "I'm not a child."

"I know, Baba. You tell me what you need."

Then Pradeep called his sister in Nashik. "I can't do every weekday. Can you manage the grab-bar fitting and the doctor's appointment?" She agreed. Yamini, tired as she was, offered to take lunch over at one.

At nine-thirty Pradeep asked his father, "Shall I help you shave, or will you do it?"

"I'll do it."

Pradeep watched, only holding the mirror. He reached the office at 9:58.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when his father called at seven?
qa.a: Pradeep felt worried and pulled three ways, between his father, his tired wife and the ten o'clock presentation.

qa.q: How did Pradeep balance the demands of that morning?
qa.a: He went to his father first, shared tasks with his sister and Yamini, and still reached work on time.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's father feel when asked whether he wants to shave himself?
qa.a: He likely feels respected and less like a child, since he had just said he didn't want fuss.

grounding: Shows a young husband balancing career, spouse and a parent's care, splitting tasks with his sister and keeping his father's dignity.
